issue_context.title: pandas.DataFrame.filter does not work with regex on a multi-index dataframe
issue_context.body:
- [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.

- [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the latest version of pandas.

#### Code Sample, a copy-pastable example

```python
df = pd.DataFrame(
      [["bar", "one", 'test'], ["bar", "one1", 'test']],
      columns=["first", "second", "third"]
)

# Single-index dataframe. Regex works as expected
df.set_index(['second']).filter( regex='e$', axis=0 )
       first third
second            
one      bar  test

# Multi-index dataframe. Regex does not work
df.set_index(['first','second']).filter( regex='e$', axis=0 )
Empty DataFrame
Columns: [third]
Index: []
```

#### Problem description
The regex expression does not work if the dataframe is multi-index.

#### Expected Output
```
             third
first second      
bar   one     test
```

comments:
looks like a duplicate of #23541

from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/23541#issuecomment-437164914

> @jreback I think what @WillAyd was looking for was a way to do inexact matching on the labels for columns that are backed by a MultiIndex. The current filter() only works for columns backed by a regular Index.
The docs could maybe be updated in the interim to clarify that filter does not work on a MultiIndex.

`filter` does seem to work on a multi-index frame provided there are no special regex characters in the `regex` parameter

```
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(
...       [["bare", "on", 'test'], ["bar", "one1", 'test']],
...       columns=["first", "second", "third"]
... )

>>> df.set_index(['first','second']).filter( regex='e', axis=0 )
             third
first second      
bare  on      test
bar   one1    test
```

If the idea is to deprecate `filter` altogether, it is fine.

I ended up using `.loc` on a specific level, but it feels somewhat cumbersome to do something like this
```
df.loc[ df.index.get_level_values( level ).str.endswith( filter ) ]
```

> `filter` does seem to work on a multi-index frame provided there are no special regex characters in the `regex` parameter

okay. removed inappropriate labels. contributions welcome to fix.

1. As it turns out DataFrame.filter did not indeed have any multi-index functionality. The reason some multi-indexes seemed to pass were because all **bytes and non-strings were converted to str**. Thus when a tuple was passed instead of a string 
```
>>> pd.core.dtypes.common.ensure_str(('bare',   'on'))
"('bare', 'on')"
```
This allows some regexes to work ( regex='e' ) but will fail for others ( regex='e$' ). 

2. Secondly, I went with the design choice that in MultiIndex the **regex or like or items function runs the checks along all values of a MultiIndex tuple** instead of an Index string. Depending on the value of the **argument "multi"** the code evaluates wether all the values of the tuple must meet the conditions or any of them. This new functionality works as such 

```
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(
...             [["bare", "on", 'test'], 
...              ["bar", "owner", 'test']], 
...             columns=["first", "second", "third"])

>>> df = df.set_index(['first','second'])

>>> items = ["bare", "on", "bar"]

>>> df.filter(items, axis=0, multi="any");        
first second third     
bare  on      test
bar   owner   test

>>> df.filter(items, axis=0, multi="all");        
first second third     
bare  on      test

```
Thus if **all** the tuple values need to be in the items list only the **first row** makes the cut whereas if **any** value of the tuple can be in items **both of the rows** are included. By default **multi = 'all'** because that makes the most sense to me. I'm open to any other implementations.

3. The new functionality works for regex, like and items conditions. Added unit tests as well. @sergiykhan your particular case could be handled as such.
```
>>> df = pd.DataFrame(
...       [["bar", "one", 'test'], ["bar", "one1", 'test']],
...       columns=["first", "second", "third"]
... )
>>> df.set_index(['first','second']).filter( regex='e$', axis=0, multi='any' )
             third
first second      
bar   one     test

```
This looks great to me. Thank you.
